description: I’m Bruno, a Brazilian high school student interested in entrepreneurship, storytelling, and making complex ideas accessible. I’m creating an interactive website about NASA equipment left on the Moon and Mars, exploring the discoveries and human stories behind it. I bring research, bilingual communication, and content creation skills. Looking for curious teammates interested in space, web development, design, or science communication. Beginners welcome—let’s build something meaningful together!
summary:
I developed Beyond the Mission, an interactive educational website that introduces school-age space enthusiasts to the stories behind NASA’s equipment and its scientific legacy.

The demo features three objects: the Opportunity rover, Voyager 1, and the Apollo 11 laser retroreflector. Visitors choose an object and explore its purpose, journey, technology, discoveries, and current status through clickable topics, images, and accessible first-person storytelling grounded in NASA resources.

The project addresses “Abandoned but Not Forgotten” by showing that equipment far from Earth is more than hardware left behind. Some missions have ended, while other instruments and spacecraft continue contributing to science.

Beyond the Mission makes these stories approachable for younger audiences, connecting how equipment works with what it helped humanity learn. The prototype establishes a format that could expand into a larger collection of missions, instruments, and interactive learning experiences.
details:
Beyond the Mission is an interactive educational website that helps school-age space enthusiasts discover the stories behind NASA’s equipment and the science it made possible. I developed it as a solo participant, combining research, visual storytelling, and AI-assisted web development.

HOW IT WORKS

Visitors enter through an introductory page and select “Start Discovering” to browse a collection carousel. The demo includes three complete stories: Opportunity, Voyager 1, and the Apollo 11 laser retroreflector. Two additional entries are clearly marked “Coming Soon.”

After selecting an object, visitors explore five clickable topics: why it was sent, its journey, how it works, its discoveries, and where it is now. This structure lets students follow their curiosity instead of reading a long article from beginning to end.

The retroreflector story also includes an interactive calculator. Visitors adjust the round-trip travel time of a light pulse and see the corresponding Earth–Moon distance. The calculator is explicitly identified as an educational demonstration, not a live measurement.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

The project connects recognizable space equipment with the scientific questions it helped answer. Opportunity introduces evidence of ancient water on Mars; Voyager 1 connects planetary discoveries with interstellar exploration; and the Apollo 11 retroreflector demonstrates how a passive instrument can support decades of research.

The intended impact is to make space history and scientific concepts more approachable, encourage independent exploration, and help younger audiences understand why these objects matter. The prototype’s educational impact has not yet been formally evaluated with students.

TOOLS AND DEVELOPMENT

The website uses HTML for structure, CSS for visual design and responsive layouts, and JavaScript for navigation, the collection carousel, topic panels, and the calculator. It is hosted through ChatGPT Sites and runs in a web browser without requiring visitors to install an application.

NASA and ILRS resources provided scientific information and imagery. Google Fonts supplied the DM Sans and Space Grotesk typefaces.

I developed the concept, selected the objects, conducted initial research, sketched the navigation, and provided review feedback. ChatGPT and OpenAI Codex assisted with research organization, English writing, translation, code generation, and implementation. AI/SI assistance is acknowledged in the website’s visible disclosure, source code, and metadata. NASA imagery and source scientific information are distinguished from AI-assisted text and code.

CREATIVE APPROACH AND DESIGN CONSIDERATIONS

The website presents each object through first-person narration, giving the experience a personal voice while clearly identifying it as a storytelling device rather than an authentic quotation. Its museum-like interface encourages visitors to choose an object and investigate its story.

The three objects represent different scientific legacies: a completed mission, an ongoing journey, and an instrument that remains useful without an onboard power supply. This avoids treating every object far from Earth as broken or forgotten.

I prioritized clear explanations, source attribution, readable layouts, and a manageable scope for a solo prototype. The site distinguishes evidence of water from evidence of life, and scientific measurements from illustrative calculations.

The current version uses images rather than rotatable 3D models. Future development could add suitable 3D assets, more equipment stories, additional learning activities, and testing with students and educators.
